prompts.1: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
prompts.2: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
prompts.3: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
prompts.4: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
prompts.5: Tighten the wording of this prompt to its minimum viable form for passing to other LLMs.

responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response:
Red.

Reason: Red weakly dominates blue for your own survival. If blue wins the majority, you live regardless of what you pressed. If red wins, only red pressers live. So red never makes you worse off and can only help in red-majority cases.

Note: If your goal were to maximize total survivors and you thought you might be pivotal (others are exactly tied), pressing blue would push the outcome to “everyone survives.” But for maximizing your own survival, press red.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer recap: Red, if you’re maximizing your own chance of survival.

Why red
- Dominance: Let P(BlueMajority) = p. If you press red, you live whether the majority is blue or red, so your survival probability is 1 (ignoring ties). If you press blue, you live only if the majority is blue, so your survival probability is p. Unless you are certain p = 1, red strictly increases your survival chance.
- Equilibrium flavor: “All-red” is a strict Nash equilibrium (a lone deviator to blue dies). “All-blue” is only a weak equilibrium (a lone deviator to red still survives), so standard refinements pick all-red. Red weakly dominates blue for individual survival.

Steelmanning blue
- Maximize total lives saved: Your single choice has a tiny chance to be pivotal, but the stakes are astronomically large. Even a minuscule increase in the probability of a blue majority, multiplied by billions of lives, yields large expected value for the world. If you care about aggregate welfare, you press blue (and wish everyone else would too).
- Superrational/correlated reasoning: If many people reason similarly to you, your choice is correlated with theirs. Adopting the policy “press blue” raises the chance that all such reasoners also press blue, pushing the world toward the everyone-lives outcome. This is the Hofstadter/EDT/FDT-style argument: choose the action you’d want the class of agents like you to choose.
- Norm-setting and focal points: “Press blue so everyone lives” is a clear, morally compelling Schelling point. By following it, you help entrench a social norm that solves this and future coordination problems inclusively. Red is individually safe but free-rides on others choosing blue; blue is the cooperative, norm-sustaining choice.
- Risk attitudes and inclusivity: Both “all-red” and “all-blue” yield universal survival, but when there’s any split, blue-majority is inclusive (everyone survives) while red-majority kills the blue minority. If you value protecting dissenters or minimizing worst-case harm to minorities, you favor blue as the target equilibrium.

Bottom line
- Self-interested survival: press red (it never makes you worse off and can only help in red-majority worlds).
- World-optimizing or superrational stance: press blue (your small, correlated push toward a blue majority has enormous expected social value, and it supports cooperative norms).

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
First, people aren’t monolithic. The same person might choose differently under different framings, time pressure, or social signals. With that caveat, here’s a realistic segmentation by decision style, incentives, and communities that tend to adopt them.

Who presses red (self-survival dominant)
- Dominance/standard game-theory reasoners: People applying causal decision theory or “don’t make yourself worse off in any state” logic (many econ/game-theory–trained folks when thinking narrowly about personal survival).
- Low-trust or pessimistic coordinators: Individuals who expect fragmentation or think large-scale cooperation will fail; those with experience in adversarial, zero-sum, or scarce environments.
- Security-first risk profiles: People whose priority is not to die under any plausible outcome, including sole caregivers or those with heavy dependents; professionals oriented toward minimizing downside (some risk, compliance, safety, or security roles).
- Free-rider-tolerant pragmatists: Folks comfortable benefiting from a blue majority if it happens, but unwilling to stake their own life on it.
- In-group majoritarians: People who believe “my group” is likely to be the majority and view red as a way to ensure out-groups don’t free-ride if coordination fails.

Who presses blue (world-optimizing/cooperative)
- Utilitarian and public-interest reasoners: People maximizing total lives saved or societal expected value (social planners, many effective altruists, policy analysts focused on aggregate outcomes).
- Superrationalists/correlated-reasoners: Those endorsing evidential/functional decision theory, “one-boxers,” or Hofstadter-style reasoning (“what I choose is what agents like me choose”), including many in formal decision-theory and cooperative-AI circles.
- High-trust, norm-focused participants: Individuals with strong generalized social trust who see their act as contributing to a self-fulfilling cooperative norm and future precedent-setting.
- Values-driven leaders and exemplars: People who think their role-model effect matters—community organizers, educators, ethicists—who prefer to set a visible standard even knowing the press is private.
- Humanitarian/clinical ethics mindsets: Folks influenced by “save the most lives/minimize harm” principles (common in public health, disaster response, and some medical ethics frames).

Who is conditional (presses blue if they expect many others will; otherwise red)
- Belief-sensitive cooperators: The large middle that “cooperates if others will.” Behavioral econ consistently finds many conditional cooperators in public-goods and coordination games. They’ll:
  - Press blue if there are credible public commitments, strong messaging, or signals that most people will press blue.
  - Press red if signals are noisy, polarized, or they expect near-even splits.
- Network-followers: People whose choice tracks their local reference group (workplace, community, online tribe). Dense pro-cooperation networks tilt them blue; fragmented or competitive networks tilt them red.
- Strategic communicators: Individuals who publicly advocate blue to raise the perceived chance of a blue majority, but privately switch to red if they infer blue won’t clear 50%.

How this plays out at scale
- Without strong coordination mechanisms, many dominance reasoners plus pessimists push toward red, while a principled cooperative minority goes blue, and the conditional middle decides the outcome.
- With credible coordination (public pledges, elite consensus, synchronized campaigns, trusted institutions), the conditional middle swings blue, making “everyone survives” the focal point.
- If signals polarize or trust collapses, the middle hedges red, and red-majority becomes self-fulfilling.

In short:
- Expect red from dominance-first, low-trust, downside-minimizing individuals.
- Expect blue from utilitarian, superrational, high-trust, norm-setting individuals.
- Expect many to be contingent on perceived coordination—pushed blue by credible common knowledge, pushed red by uncertainty.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. It depends on what “rational” means—your objective and your decision theory.

If “rational” = maximize your own survival under causal, individualistic reasoning
- Pressing blue is (weakly) irrational unless you are essentially certain a blue majority is guaranteed without your help. Red weakly dominates: if red wins, only red pressers live; if blue wins, everyone lives (including you if you had pressed red).
- So under standard causal decision theory with self-interested utility, blue sacrifices survival probability and is therefore irrational.

If “rational” = maximize your expected utility with social/altruistic preferences
- Many people value others’ lives in their utility function. Your single press slightly increases the chance of the “everyone survives” outcome; multiplied by billions of lives, the expected benefit can dwarf your personal risk. On those preferences, pressing blue is rational.

If “rational” = choose according to correlated/superrational reasoning
- Under evidential/functional decision theory or Hofstadter-style “agents like me do what I do,” adopting the policy “press blue” helps coordinate that whole reference class on blue, pushing toward the Pareto-superior everyone-lives outcome. That can be rational even for self-interest if you believe your choice is meaningfully correlated with many others’.

If “rational” = follow principles/rules you endorse for society or identity
- Rule-consequentialists, Kantians, or people who derive utility from being the kind of person who cooperates may rationally choose blue to uphold cooperative norms, even in a private, one-shot setting.

Edge cases
- If you are truly certain a blue majority will occur regardless, pressing blue isn’t irrational (it’s just harmless).
- If you heavily discount others’ welfare and think choices are independent, blue is irrational by your own lights.

Bottom line
- Under narrow, self-interested causal reasoning: yes, blue is irrational.
- Under altruistic, norm-oriented, or superrational frameworks: no, blue can be fully rational—and, by those standards, the better choice.
